lec05kp16-u01-p1-title.name: u01-p1-title
lec05kp16-u01-p1-title.text: A different kind of new coordinate: each node answers only near its own centre

lec05kp16-u01-p1-bridge.name: u01-p1-bridge
lec05kp16-u01-p1-bridge.text: The products of KP15 respond over the whole space. Can the new coordinates be nodes that respond only to data nearby?

lec05kp16-u01-p1-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp16-bumps
lec05kp16-u01-p1-fig1.text: Top: one sigmoid answers along the whole line; bottom: three Gaussian nodes answer near their centres at −2, 0 and 2.

image.alt: Top: one sigmoid answers along the whole line; bottom: three Gaussian nodes answer near their centres at −2, 0 and 2.

lec05kp16-u01-p1-term:徑向基函數.name: term:Radial basis function
lec05kp16-u01-p1-term:徑向基函數.text: **Radial basis function** (RBF): a function of the distance to a centre $c_i$, most often Gaussian, $\exp\!\big(-\|x-c_i\|^2/2\sigma_i^2\big)$.

lec05kp16-u01-p1-c1.name: u01-p1-c1
lec05kp16-u01-p1-c1.text: **RBF network**: $g(x)=w_0+\sum_{i=1}^{k}w_i\exp\!\big(-\|x-c_i\|^2/2\sigma_i^2\big)$, one layer of Gaussian hidden nodes and a linear output.

lec05kp16-u01-p1-c2.name: u01-p1-c2
lec05kp16-u01-p1-c2.text: **Kin of the Parzen estimate**: almost the same form, but Parzen uses one kernel per training point ($k=N$) while here $k\ll N$.

lec05kp16-u01-p2-title.name: u01-p2-title
lec05kp16-u01-p2-title.text: The equal-output lines of a sigmoid are straight and those of an RBF are circles: local against global

lec05kp16-u01-p2-bridge.name: u01-p2-bridge
lec05kp16-u01-p2-bridge.text: One sigmoid answers along the whole line while each Gaussian answers only near its centre. In two dimensions, what shapes do their equal-output sets take?

lec05kp16-u01-p2-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp16-contours
lec05kp16-u01-p2-fig1.text: Left: the equal-output lines of a sigmoid node are parallel straight lines; right: those of an RBF node are concentric circles around its centre.

image.alt: Left: the equal-output lines of a sigmoid node are parallel straight lines; right: those of an RBF node are concentric circles around its centre.

lec05kp16-u01-p2-term:局部反應.name: term:Local response
lec05kp16-u01-p2-term:局部反應.text: **Local response**: a node answers only near its centre and fades to 0 away from it. By contrast a **global response** follows a whole hyperplane.

lec05kp16-u01-p2-c1.name: u01-p2-c1
lec05kp16-u01-p2-c1.text: **Equal-output sets**: a sigmoid node has a whole hyperplane (a line in two dimensions); an RBF node has a hypersphere (a circle).

lec05kp16-u01-p2-c2.name: u01-p2-c2
lec05kp16-u01-p2-c2.text: **Example** ($2\sigma^2=1$): at distances 0, 1, 2, 3 from the centre the Gaussian answers $1,\ 0.368,\ 0.0183,\ 0.000123$.

lec05kp16-u01-p3-title.name: u01-p3-title
lec05kp16-u01-p3-title.text: XOR needs only two centres: (1,0) and (0,1) fold onto one point

lec05kp16-u01-p3-bridge.name: u01-p3-bridge
lec05kp16-u01-p3-bridge.text: An RBF node has circles as equal-output sets and its response fades with distance. How few centres does it need to solve XOR?

lec05kp16-u01-p3-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp16-xormap
lec05kp16-u01-p3-fig1.text: Left: the four XOR points and the centres (1,1), (0,0) on the input plane; right: after the map (1,0) and (0,1) coincide at (0.368,0.368) and the line y₁+y₂=1 separates the classes.

image.alt: Left: the four XOR points and the centres (1,1), (0,0) on the input plane; right: after the map (1,0) and (0,1) coincide at (0.368,0.368) and the line y₁+y₂=1 separates the classes.

lec05kp16-u01-p4-title.name: u01-p4-title
lec05kp16-u01-p4-title.text: The line in the feature space is a closed curve in the original space

lec05kp16-u01-p4-bridge.name: u01-p4-bridge
lec05kp16-u01-p4-bridge.text: One line separates the points folded onto one point. Back on the original plane, what does it become?

lec05kp16-u01-p4-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp16-xorcurve
lec05kp16-u01-p4-fig1.text: On the original plane g(x)=0 is a closed curve around (0,0) and (1,1), with (1,0) and (0,1) outside it.

image.alt: On the original plane g(x)=0 is a closed curve around (0,0) and (1,1), with (1,0) and (0,1) outside it.

lec05kp16-u01-p4-c1.name: u01-p4-c1
lec05kp16-u01-p4-c1.text: **Boundary**: $g(x)=e^{-\|x-c_1\|^2}+e^{-\|x-c_2\|^2}-1=0$ is a closed curve around the two centres.

lec05kp16-u01-p4-c2.name: u01-p4-c2
lec05kp16-u01-p4-c2.text: **$g$ at the four points**: $+0.135$ at $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$ (inside the curve) and $-0.264$ at $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ (outside).

lec05kp16-u01-p4-c3.name: u01-p4-c3
lec05kp16-u01-p4-c3.text: **The default side**: far from every centre $g\to-1$, so faraway points all fall on the outside class.

lec05kp16-u01-p5-title.name: u01-p5-title
lec05kp16-u01-p5-title.text: With the centres fixed the weights are a linear problem: 99.5% on the rings with k=16 centres

lec05kp16-u01-p5-bridge.name: u01-p5-bridge
lec05kp16-u01-p5-bridge.text: Two centres solved XOR with a closed curve in the original space. With more complicated data, how many centres are needed and how are the weights learned?

lec05kp16-u01-p5-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp16-ringsk
lec05kp16-u01-p5-fig1.text: Accuracy on the concentric rings with random centres against the number of centres k: 91.5% at k=8, 99.5% at k=16 and 99.9% at k=32.

image.alt: Accuracy on the concentric rings with random centres against the number of centres k: 91.5% at k=8, 99.5% at k=16 and 99.9% at k=32.

lec05kp16-u01-p5-term:固定中心.name: term:Fixed centres
lec05kp16-u01-p5-term:固定中心.text: **Fixed centres**: pick $k$ training points at random as the centres. With the centres fixed only $w$ remains, the linear problem of KP13 (least squares).

lec05kp16-u01-p5-c1.name: u01-p5-c1
lec05kp16-u01-p5-c1.text: **Experiment** (designed here): concentric rings (an inner ring of radius about 1 and an outer about 2.2), 200 training points and 500 held-out new points, $\sigma^2=0.5$, averaged over 20 random choices for each $k$.

lec05kp16-u01-p5-c2.name: u01-p5-c2
lec05kp16-u01-p5-c2.text: **Result** (new points): $k=2$ gives 64.2%, $k=8$ gives 91.5%, $k=16$ gives 99.5% and $k=32$ gives 99.9%.

lec05kp16-u01-p6-title.name: u01-p6-title
lec05kp16-u01-p6-title.text: Clustering the centres: 95.0% at k=8 on two moons against 93.3% for random picks, and steadier

lec05kp16-u01-p6-bridge.name: u01-p6-bridge
lec05kp16-u01-p6-bridge.text: Random centres reach 99.5% on the rings at $k=16$. Can the centres be chosen more cleverly for a steadier result?

lec05kp16-u01-p6-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp16-centers
lec05kp16-u01-p6-fig1.text: Accuracy on new points for random centres and k-means centres on two moons (mean and sd): 93.3% against 95.0% at k=8.

image.alt: Accuracy on new points for random centres and k-means centres on two moons (mean and sd): 93.3% against 95.0% at k=8.

lec05kp16-u01-p6-term:分群.name: term:Clustering
lec05kp16-u01-p6-term:分群.text: **Clustering** (k-means here): split the data into $k$ groups, use each group mean as a centre, then learn $w$ with supervised least squares.

lec05kp16-u01-p6-c1.name: u01-p6-c1
lec05kp16-u01-p6-c1.text: **Experiment** (designed here): two moons of 60 points each with noise, 500 new points, $\sigma^2=0.3$, 20 repeats each.

lec05kp16-u01-p6-c2.name: u01-p6-c2
lec05kp16-u01-p6-c2.text: **Result** (new points): $k=6$: 90.5% against 92.7%; $k=8$: 93.3% (sd 0.018) against 95.0% (0.004); at $k=2,4$ random is slightly higher.

lec05kp16-u01-p7-title.name: u01-p7-title
lec05kp16-u01-p7-title.text: The price of locality is dimension: at l=10 100 centres reach only 40% of the points

lec05kp16-u01-p7-bridge.name: u01-p7-bridge
lec05kp16-u01-p7-bridge.text: Clustering the centres made them steadier on two moons. But a local response only reaches near the centres, so as the dimension grows, are the centres still enough?

lec05kp16-u01-p7-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp16-curse
lec05kp16-u01-p7-fig1.text: Fraction of test points with a response above 0.1 for 100 random centres: 100% for l=1, 2, 5, 40% for l=10 and 0% for l=20.

image.alt: Fraction of test points with a response above 0.1 for 100 random centres: 100% for l=1, 2, 5, 40% for l=10 and 0% for l=20.

lec05kp16-u01-p7-term:維度詛咒.name: term:Curse of dimensionality
lec05kp16-u01-p7-term:維度詛咒.text: **Curse of dimensionality**: as the dimension grows the number of points or centres needed to fill the space grows exponentially, while the data and the centres are never enough.

lec05kp16-u01-p7-c1.name: u01-p7-c1
lec05kp16-u01-p7-c1.text: **Experiment** (designed here): 100 random centres in the unit cube, $\sigma=0.3$; median nearest-centre distance for $l=2,5,10,20$: $0.05,\,0.30,\,0.67,\,1.22$.

lec05kp16-u01-p7-c2.name: u01-p7-c2
lec05kp16-u01-p7-c2.text: **Result**: test points with a response $>0.1$: 100% for $l\le5$, 40% for $l=10$ and 0% for $l=20$. A grid of 5 centres per axis needs 25, 3125 and 9,765,625 centres ($l=2,5,10$).

lec05kp16-u01-p8-title.name: u01-p8-title
lec05kp16-u01-p8-title.text: The MLP asks which side, the RBF how close: global against local

lec05kp16-u01-p8-bridge.name: u01-p8-bridge
lec05kp16-u01-p8-bridge.text: Local response reaches only 40% of the points at $l=10$, the price of dimension. Put side by side, what are the strengths and weaknesses of the MLP and the RBF?

lec05kp16-u01-p8-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp16-compare
lec05kp16-u01-p8-fig1.text: Comparison table of the MLP and the RBF network: node argument, equal-output set, response, learning speed, sparse-data generalization and nodes needed.

image.alt: Comparison table of the MLP and the RBF network: node argument, equal-output set, response, learning speed, sparse-data generalization and nodes needed.

lec05kp16-u01-p8-c1.name: u01-p8-c1
lec05kp16-u01-p8-c1.text: **Node and response**: the MLP node is $\sum_jw_jx_j$ with hyperplanes and a global response; the RBF is $\|x-c_i\|$ with hyperspheres and a local one.

lec05kp16-u01-p8-c2.name: u01-p8-c2
lec05kp16-u01-p8-c2.text: **Learning and generalization** (source): the RBF learns faster; the MLP generalizes better where training data are sparse; for the same accuracy the RBF needs many more nodes.

lec05kp16-u01-p8-c3.name: u01-p8-c3
lec05kp16-u01-p8-c3.text: **To remember**: the MLP thinks in terms of which side of a hyperplane, the RBF in terms of how close to a centre. Local learns fast but is hungry for dimensions.

lec05kp16-u01-p9-title.name: u01-p9-title
lec05kp16-u01-p9-title.text: Extension: six ways to choose the centres, from random picks to support vectors and growing

lec05kp16-u01-p9-bridge.name: u01-p9-bridge
lec05kp16-u01-p9-bridge.text: The MLP and the RBF each have strengths and weaknesses, and the difficulty of the RBF is choosing the centres. Besides random picks and clustering, what other ways are there?

lec05kp16-u01-p9-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp16-ways
lec05kp16-u01-p9-fig1.text: Six ways to choose the centres: fixed centres, trained centres, clustering, orthogonal least squares, support vectors and growing.

image.alt: Six ways to choose the centres: fixed centres, trained centres, clustering, orthogonal least squares, support vectors and growing.

lec05kp16-u01-p9-c1.name: u01-p9-c1
lec05kp16-u01-p9-c1.text: **Train the centres**: learn $w_i,c_i,\sigma_i$ together by gradient descent, too costly for many uses.

lec05kp16-u01-p9-c2.name: u01-p9-c2
lec05kp16-u01-p9-c2.text: **Orthogonal least squares**: start from many candidates and pick a compact set by forward regression, which also estimates $k$.

lec05kp16-u01-p9-c3.name: u01-p9-c3
lec05kp16-u01-p9-c3.text: **Support vectors**: view the RBF network as a kernel map; training is a quadratic programme with a global optimum and the number of centres decided automatically. **Growing**: a new sample far from every centre with a large error becomes a new centre (source).

lec05kp16-u01-p10-title.name: u01-p10-title
lec05kp16-u01-p10-title.text: Extension: practice, map a middle point and a faraway point

lec05kp16-u01-p10-bridge.name: u01-p10-bridge
lec05kp16-u01-p10-bridge.text: There are six ways to choose the centres. Back to the two centres of XOR, where do a middle point and a faraway point map and which class do they get?

lec05kp16-u01-p10-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp16-practice
lec05kp16-u01-p10-fig1.text: Practice figure: centres (1,1), (0,0) and g=y₁+y₂−1; map (0.5,0.5) and (3,3) and classify them.

image.alt: Practice figure: centres (1,1), (0,0) and g=y₁+y₂−1; map (0.5,0.5) and (3,3) and classify them.

lec05kp16-u01-p10-q2.name: u01-p10-q2
lec05kp16-u01-p10-q2.text: **Question 2**: do the same for the faraway point $(3,3)$.

lec05kp16-u01-p11-title.name: u01-p11-title
lec05kp16-u01-p11-title.text: Extension: worked solution of questions 1 and 2

lec05kp16-u01-p11-bridge.name: u01-p11-bridge
lec05kp16-u01-p11-bridge.text: The practice asked to map the middle point $(0.5,0.5)$ and the faraway point $(3,3)$ and classify them. Worked out in full, what are the answers?

lec05kp16-u01-p11-a2.name: u01-p11-a2
lec05kp16-u01-p11-a2.text: **Question 2**: squared distances 8 and 18 give $y=(0.0003,\,1.5\times10^{-8})$ and $g\approx-1.0<0$, so $\omega_2$.

lec05kp16-u01-p11-a3.name: u01-p11-a3
lec05kp16-u01-p11-a3.text: **Check**: the middle point lies between the centres, inside the curve; the faraway point falls to the bias $-1$ and takes the default class.

steps.label: RBF networks
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Main line 8 pages plus 3 extension pages (not timed). Self-study deck, English version. Made under CLARITY.md C12 to C18. The RBF form, the two centres for XOR (0.135, 0.368), the local-against-global comparison table and the centre-selection methods follow the source; the experiments on the number of centres for rings and moons, random against k-means, and the dimension experiment on locality were recomputed by a program and designed for this lecture (added). Speaker notes are published with the file and contain no student numbers, grades or exam items.

steps.label: Gaussian nodes
steps.speakerNotes: The products of KP15 respond over the whole space. This page asks whether the new coordinates can be nodes that respond only to data nearby. One term first: a radial basis function, RBF for short, is a function of the distance to a centre, most often Gaussian. An RBF network is g equal to w0 plus the sum of weights times Gaussians, one layer of Gaussian hidden nodes and a linear output. It is close kin of the Parzen estimate, almost the same form, but Parzen uses one kernel per training point, k equal to N, while here k is much smaller than N. The figure contrasts a sigmoid: one sigmoid answers along the whole line while each of three Gaussians answers only near its centre. The next page shows how this difference looks in two dimensions.

steps.label: Local against global
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed one sigmoid answering along the whole line while each Gaussian answers only near its centre. This page asks what shapes their equal-output sets take in two dimensions. First local response: a node answers only near its centre and fades to 0 away from it; a global response instead follows a whole hyperplane. A sigmoid node has a whole hyperplane as its equal-output set, a line in two dimensions; an RBF node has a hypersphere, a circle. Example: with 2 sigma squared equal to 1, at distances 0, 1, 2 and 3 from the centre the Gaussian answers 1, 0.368, 0.0183 and 0.000123. The next page solves XOR with an RBF that has only two centres.

steps.label: XOR with two centres
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said an RBF node has circles as equal-output sets and its response fades with distance. This page asks how few centres it needs to solve XOR. The answer is two: centres at (1,1) and (0,0), and the function e to the minus squared distance. The map: (0,0) goes to (0.135, 1), (1,1) goes to (1, 0.135), and both (1,0) and (0,1) go to (0.368, 0.368), folded onto one point again. g equal to y1 plus y2 minus 1 gives +0.135 for the first two points and -0.264 for the other two, so one line separates them. The next page shows what that line becomes in the original space.

steps.label: Back in the original space
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed a line separating the folded points. This page asks what that line becomes on the original plane. g equal to e to the minus squared distance to centre 1 plus e to the minus squared distance to centre 2 minus 1 equal to 0 is a closed curve around the two centres. The four values of g: +0.135 at (0,0) and (1,1), inside the curve, and -0.264 at (1,0) and (0,1), outside it. Far from every centre g tends to -1, so faraway points all fall on the outside class, a property of local response. The next page asks how the weights are learned and how many centres are needed.

steps.label: Fixed centres
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said two centres solved XOR exactly. This page asks how many centres are needed and how the weights are learned for more complicated data. First fixed centres: pick k training points at random as the centres. With the centres fixed only w remains, the linear problem of KP13, solved by least squares. The experiment was designed here: concentric rings with 200 training and 500 new points, sigma squared 0.5, averaged over 20 random choices for each k. The accuracy on new points is 64.2% for k equal to 2, 91.5% for 8, 99.5% for 16 and 99.9% for 32. The next page asks whether the centres can be chosen more cleverly.

steps.label: Choosing the centres
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that random centres reach 99.5% on the rings at k equal to 16. This page asks whether the centres can be chosen more cleverly for a steadier result. First clustering: here k-means splits the data into k groups, uses each group mean as a centre and then learns w by supervised least squares, a mix of unsupervised and supervised learning. The experiment was designed here: two moons of 60 points each with noise, 500 new points, sigma squared 0.3, 20 repeats each. The accuracy on new points is 90.5% against 92.7% at k equal to 6 and 93.3% with standard deviation 0.018 against 95.0% with 0.004 at k equal to 8; at k equal to 2 random is slightly higher. So clustering is mainly steadier, not always more accurate. The next page asks what the price of local response is.

steps.label: The price of locality
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said clustering made the centres steadier. This page asks whether the centres are still enough when the input dimension grows, since a local response only reaches near the centres. First the curse of dimensionality: as the dimension grows the number of points or centres needed to fill the space grows exponentially. The experiment was designed here: 100 random centres in the unit cube, sigma 0.3 and 2000 test points; the median distance to the nearest centre for l equal to 2, 5, 10 and 20 is 0.05, 0.30, 0.67 and 1.22. Test points with a response above 0.1: 100% for l up to 5, 40% for l equal to 10 and 0% for l equal to 20. A grid of 5 centres per axis needs 25, 3125 and 9,765,625 centres. Locality makes RBF learn fast but it also makes it hungry for dimensions. The next page puts the MLP and the RBF side by side.

steps.label: MLP against RBF
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said local response reaches only 40% of the points at l equal to 10, the price of dimension. This page puts the MLP and the RBF side by side, and the table comes from the source. Node and response: the MLP node is the inner product of w and x with hyperplanes as equal-output sets and a global response; the RBF is the distance to a centre with hyperspheres and a local response. Learning and generalization: the RBF learns faster; the MLP generalizes better where training data are sparse; for the same accuracy the RBF needs many more nodes. To remember: the MLP thinks in terms of which side of a hyperplane, the RBF in terms of how close to a centre; local learns fast but is hungry for dimensions. The next extension page looks at other ways to choose the centres.

steps.label: Extension: other ways
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the MLP and the RBF each have strengths and weaknesses and that the difficulty of the RBF is choosing the centres. This extension asks what other ways there are besides random picks and clustering. The source lists: training the centres, learning the weights, centres and widths together by gradient descent, too costly for many uses; orthogonal least squares, which starts from many candidates and picks a compact set by forward regression, also estimating k; support vectors, viewing the RBF network as a kernel map, with a quadratic programme that has a global optimum and decides the number of centres automatically; and growing, where a new sample far from every centre with a large error becomes a new centre. The figure lists all six ways. The next page poses an exercise.

steps.label: Extension: practice
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page listed six ways to choose the centres. This page poses an exercise: back to the two centres of XOR, c1 equal to (1,1) and c2 equal to (0,0), the function e to the minus squared distance, and g equal to y1 plus y2 minus 1 with g above 0 meaning omega 1. Question 1: map the middle point (0.5, 0.5) to y and find its class; the hint is that its squared distance to both centres is 0.5. Question 2: do the same for the faraway point (3, 3). Work it out first, then see the next page.

steps.label: Extension: solution
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page posed the exercise and this page is the complete solution. Question 1: y is e to the minus 0.5 for both, which is (0.607, 0.607), and g is 0.607 plus 0.607 minus 1, which is +0.213, above 0, so omega 1. Question 2: the squared distances are 8 and 18, y is (0.0003, 2 times 10 to the minus 8) and g is about -1.0, below 0, so omega 2. Check: the middle point lies between the centres, inside the curve; the faraway point falls to the bias -1 and takes the default class. That finishes RBF networks; the next knowledge point looks at the universal approximation theorem.

metadata.title: Pattern Recognition, Chapter 4, KP16: RBF networks, local against global response (undergraduate, self-study)
